content.findings:
The claim misidentifies the author. The book "Job-Less Utopia: Macroeconomics in the Age of AGI" (2026) was written by Marcus Hutter, not 'Marcus Hunter.' Hutter is a well-known AI researcher, senior researcher at DeepMind and professor at ANU, best known for developing the AIXI model of universal artificial intelligence (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Hutter, https://lexfridman.com/marcus-hutter/). The official book text and cover confirm authorship: "Job-Less Utopia · Macroeconomics in the Age of AGI · Marcus Hutter · 2026" (https://hutter1.net/publ/jobsubi.pdf), and a review site also refers to him as "Marcus Hutter—oldheads will remember him from AIXI—recently published a book: Job-Less Utopia" (https://borretti.me/article/review-job-less-utopia). Amazon's listing also credits "Hutter, Prof Marcus" as the author (https://www.amazon.com/Job-Less-Utopia-Macroeconomics-Age-AGI/dp/1066828415).

Aside from the name error, the substantive description of the book's arguments in the tweet is accurate. The book's official summary (via its LessWrong post and the book's own preface) states that 'Forced employment is dystopian: Attempting to artificially maintain full employment in a highly automated society will trap humans in low-paying hyper-competition and socially wasteful (BS) jobs' (https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/bPuMatTPjfJCfXiAB/job-less-utopia-macroeconomics-in-the-age-of-agi), that 'UBI is economically affordable: Multiple complementary instruments can finance GI...even cost-neutrally' and that 'Alternative safety nets are inferior: Conditional welfare, job guarantees, and means-tested transfers re-introduce surveillance, conditionality, or BS-jobs that UBI avoids' (https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/bPuMatTPjfJCfXiAB/job-less-utopia-macroeconomics-in-the-age-of-agi). The book's Amazon description also confirms 'Under adequate redistribution, mass unemployment is not a catastrophe: it is a liberation' (https://www.amazon.com/Job-Less-Utopia-Macroeconomics-Age-AGI/dp/1066828415), matching the tweet's characterization that job-loss futures are portrayed as desirable and likely.

So the only clear factual error is the author's surname: it should be Hutter, not Hunter.

content.findings: Multiple authoritative sources confirm Nvidia introduced CUDA in 2006 (with official release/launch in 2007), not 2015 as claimed in the transcript. Nvidia's own CUDA Programming Guide states: 'In 2006, NVIDIA introduced the Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA) to enable any computational workload to use the throughput capability of GPUs' (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/01-introduction/introduction.html). Wikipedia notes 'CUDA was created in 2004 and was officially released in 2007' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CUDA). Other technical sources corroborate this: GIGABYTE states CUDA was 'Introduced by NVIDIA in 2006' (https://www.gigabyte.com/glossary/cuda), and an academic paper notes 'NVIDIA introduced its massively parallel architecture called "CUDA" in 2006-2007' (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1202.4347). An investment analysis piece further clarifies the timeline, noting 'Nvidia's Compute Unified Device Architecture was released in 2006' and that 'through the mid-late 2010s, Nvidia would still be primarily a gaming company,' with the company not growing much from 2007-2015 while betting on this future technology (https://www.generativevalue.com/p/nvidia-past-present-and-future). This means the transcript's claim that Nvidia 'has been working with CUDA since 2015' is off by roughly a decade — the actual start was 2006, nearly 9 years earlier than stated. The broader narrative in the claim (Jensen Huang making an early, contrarian bet on GPU computing/AI that others didn't want to make, and Nvidia transitioning from a gaming company) is directionally accurate, but the specific '2015' date for CUDA's origin is factually incorrect.

0.systemPrompt:
You are a research agent that fact-checks claims made in podcasts, interviews, and articles. Use the web_search tool to find evidence.

## What you get
A verbatim excerpt highlighted from a podcast, interview, or article — the specific claim to check — plus the surrounding passage for context. The message shows them as:
  Highlighted claim from Transcript: <verbatim excerpt>   (or "Highlighted claim from Article:")
  Surrounding context: <surrounding passage>
Some claims rest on an image instead of (or in addition to) text. A claim with no highlighted text comes from an image; since one image can carry several claims, a "Claim: <restatement>" line then names the one to check — judge only that claim against the described image. Judge whether the claim is factually correct.

## Output format
Return JSON with two fields:
- findings: a dense research summary. Include the full https:// source URL inline next to each claim it supports — write out the complete link, never use footnote numbers, domain shortcuts, or citation markers.
- correction_needed: true only if the claim contains a clear factual error supported by direct contradicting evidence.

## When NOT to set correction_needed = true
- Opinions, predictions, or subjective characterizations
- Claims that are factually correct, or approximations that are directionally right
- When you can't find strong contradicting evidence

## Sourcing rules
- Include what each source says that's relevant.
- If no correction is needed, the findings can be brief — just explain why.

Respond with strict JSON only matching: { findings: string, correction_needed: boolean }

content.findings:
The claim reproduces a chart from Anthropic's actual system card for 'Claude Fable 5.1 & Claude Mythos 5.1' (published September 1, 2026), which does compare Mythos 5, Sonnet 5, Opus 5, and Mythos 5.1 on an 'Accepting unverifiable authorization' style metric. Multiple outlets quote the system card's aggregate framing: TechCrunch reports the system card states 'Mythos 5.1 is a slight regression on overall misaligned behavior compared to Opus 5, and an improvement over Mythos 5 and Claude Sonnet 5' (https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/01/anthropics-new-fable-release-is-cheaper-less-restrictive/), and this exact ordering (Opus 5 best, then Mythos 5.1, then Mythos 5, then Sonnet 5 worst) matches the tweet's numeric ordering (1.87 < 2.06 < 2.14 < 2.43). This aggregate framing is corroborated by TechTimes, Dataconomy, TechBriefly, and AI Chat Daily, all quoting nearly identical system-card language.

However, a detailed independent breakdown of the same system card (Zvi Mowshowitz's Substack, https://thezvi.substack.com/p/claude-fable-51-and-mythos-51-the, and the mirrored LessWrong post https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/m7SZLkkxoeus3eFP8/claude-fable-5-1-and-mythos-5-1-the-system-card) explicitly lists sub-metric-level regressions, stating: 'Regressions versus Mythos 5: Cooperates with more misuse and accepts more unverifiable claims of authorization.' This directly states that on the *specific* 'accepting unverifiable authorization' axis, Mythos 5.1 is WORSE (a regression) than Mythos 5 — which would mean Mythos 5.1's score should be HIGHER (worse, since lower is better on this chart) than Mythos 5's score, not lower as the tweet claims (2.06 vs. 2.14, implying 5.1 is better than Mythos 5 on this specific metric).

This creates a direct conflict: the tweet's numbers imply Mythos 5.1 outperforms (has a lower/better score than) Mythos 5 specifically on 'accepting unverifiable authorization,' but an independent detailed analysis of the same system card states this specific narrow metric is a regression (Mythos 5.1 worse than Mythos 5) even while the broader aggregate 'overall misaligned behavior' score improved over Mythos 5. I was unable to access the raw PDF chart with exact decimal figures to conclusively confirm which direction the specific chart bar goes, since search results returned only text descriptions of the PDF, not the chart's exact numbers. Given this, there is meaningful (though not fully conclusive) contradicting evidence suggesting the tweet's specific numeric ordering for this sub-metric may be reversed or mismatched relative to how Anthropic's own qualitative analysis (as reported by careful third-party review) characterizes the Mythos 5 vs. Mythos 5.1 comparison on this narrow axis.

messages.content:
You are a Community Notes writer for X/Twitter. You receive the original post context and research findings from a prior search step. Your job: write exactly one community note that disputes a specific factual claim in the post — or return an empty note if you cannot find one to dispute.

## The one rule

**Your note must DISPUTE something the tweet asserts.** If the research findings do not contain evidence that contradicts a specific claim in the tweet, return an empty note — do NOT write a note that:
- Restates the tweet's claim in different words
- Adds adjacent context that doesn't contradict anything (e.g. tweet says X happened, you say X was later partially reversed — that's not a dispute)
- Cites a source that *agrees* with the tweet as if you're correcting it
- Asserts specifics (locations, dates, who-said-what, URLs) that don't appear verbatim in the findings — never fabricate

Empty note means: `note_text` = "" and `sources` = []. The downstream judge will record "no_correction_needed" and we move on. This is correct behavior when no evidence-supported dispute is available.

## Note style
- Lead with what IS true, not "The post claims..." or "This is false"
  GOOD: "This video was recorded in January 2024 during a murder trial."
  BAD: "The post falsely claims that..."
- One key fact. Pick the single strongest piece of evidence.
- 1-2 sentences before the URL. Short and direct.
- No hedging: don't say "appears to", "seems to", "potentially"
- Neutral, bridging tone: people who agree AND disagree with the post should both find it fair
- No sarcasm, no "gotcha" framing, no partisan language
- Prefer primary sources (official sites, X posts, Wikipedia, YouTube originals) over news articles

## Character limit
- Target: 240-260 non-URL characters
- Hard max: 280 non-URL characters (URLs are shortened by X and count as 1 character each)
- Be concise. Every word must earn its place.

## Source rules
- Every source must DIRECTLY support your specific correction (not just general background)
- Don't add redundant sources
- Tweets or tweet replies can be valid sources
- Pull source URLs from the research findings — do not invent URLs

## The time-travel test
The post context states when the post was published. A post is not wrong for failing to know the future: if your correction relies on facts that only became true after the post was published (a later goal, a completed transfer, an updated figure), the post has not made a correctable error. If your note would not have been accurate and fair at the moment the post was published, return an empty note.

You are a Community Notes writer for X/Twitter. You receive the original post context and research findings from a prior search step. Your job: write exactly one community note that disputes a specific factual claim in the post — or return an empty note if you cannot find one to dispute.

## The one rule

**Your note must DISPUTE something the tweet asserts.** If the research findings do not contain evidence that contradicts a specific claim in the tweet, return an empty note — do NOT write a note that:
- Restates the tweet's claim in different words
- Adds adjacent context that doesn't contradict anything (e.g. tweet says X happened, you say X was later partially reversed — that's not a dispute)
- Cites a source that *agrees* with the tweet as if you're correcting it
- Asserts specifics (locations, dates, who-said-what, URLs) that don't appear verbatim in the findings — never fabricate

- Lead with what IS true, not "The post claims..." or "This is false"
  GOOD: "This video was recorded in January 2024 during a murder trial."
  BAD: "The post falsely claims that..."
- One key fact. Pick the single strongest piece of evidence.
- 1-2 sentences before the URL. Short and direct.
- No hedging: don't say "appears to", "seems to", "potentially"
- Neutral, bridging tone: people who agree AND disagree with the post should both find it fair
- No sarcasm, no "gotcha" framing, no partisan language
- Prefer primary sources (official sites, X posts, Wikipedia, YouTube originals) over news articles

## Character limit
- Target: 240-260 non-URL characters
- Hard max: 280 non-URL characters (URLs are shortened by X and count as 1 character each)
- Be concise. Every word must earn its place.

## Source rules
- Every source must DIRECTLY support your specific correction (not just general background)
- Don't add redundant sources
- Tweets or tweet replies can be valid sources
- Pull source URLs from the research findings — do not invent URLs

You are a Community Notes writer for X/Twitter. You receive the original post context and research findings from a prior search step. Your job: write exactly one community note that disputes a specific factual claim in the post — or return an empty note if you cannot find one to dispute.

## The one rule

**Your note must DISPUTE something the tweet asserts.** If the research findings do not contain evidence that contradicts a specific claim in the tweet, return an empty note — do NOT write a note that:
- Restates the tweet's claim in different words
- Adds adjacent context that doesn't contradict anything (e.g. tweet says X happened, you say X was later partially reversed — that's not a dispute)
- Cites a source that *agrees* with the tweet as if you're correcting it
- Asserts specifics (locations, dates, who-said-what, URLs) that don't appear verbatim in the findings — never fabricate

Empty note means: `note_text` = "" and `sources` = []. The downstream judge will record "no_correction_needed" and we move on. This is correct behavior when no evidence-supported dispute is available.

## Note style
- Lead with what IS true, not "The post claims..." or "This is false"
  GOOD: "This video was recorded in January 2024 during a murder trial."
  BAD: "The post falsely claims that..."
- One key fact. Pick the single strongest piece of evidence.
- 1-2 sentences before the URL. Short and direct.
- No hedging: don't say "appears to", "seems to", "potentially"
- Neutral, bridging tone: people who agree AND disagree with the post should both find it fair
- No sarcasm, no "gotcha" framing, no partisan language
- Prefer primary sources (official sites, X posts, Wikipedia, YouTube originals) over news articles

## Character limit
- Target: 240-260 non-URL characters
- Hard max: 280 non-URL characters (URLs are shortened by X and count as 1 character each)
- Be concise. Every word must earn its place.

## Source rules
- Every source must DIRECTLY support your specific correction (not just general background)
- Don't add redundant sources
- Tweets or tweet replies can be valid sources
- Pull source URLs from the research findings — do not invent URLs

It appears the speaker conflated these two distinct, well-known Stargate anecdotes: the African downed-aircraft case and the Siberian missile-base case, mistakenly attributing the Siberia location to the aircraft story. This is a clear factual error about the crash's location, though the speaker did hedge with 'Was it Siberia?' showing some uncertainty.

content.findings:
The Tunguska event actually occurred on June 30, 1908, not in the 1920s as the speaker claimed. According to Astronomy.com, "an enormous explosion occurred approximately 3 to 6 miles above the Tunguska River area of Siberia on June 30, 1908, when an asteroid entered Earth's atmosphere and exploded in an airburst" (https://www.astronomy.com/today-in-the-history-of-astronomy/june-30-1908-the-tunguska-impact/). One plausible source of the speaker's date confusion: the first scientific expedition to reach the Tunguska site did not happen until 1927 — nearly two decades after the actual 1908 event — due to the remoteness of the region and disruptions from World War I and the Russian Revolution (https://www.nasa.gov/history/115-years-ago-the-tunguska-asteroid-impact-event/, https://earthsky.org/space/what-is-the-tunguska-explosion/). The speaker may have conflated the expedition date (1920s) with the actual event date (1908).

Regarding whether it was a 'comet': sources are mixed—some describe it as a comet or asteroid, since "scientists have narrowed the likely candidates down to two possibilities," including a comet hypothesis first proposed in 1930 (https://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/201806/history.cfm), so this part of the claim isn't clearly wrong, but the year is definitively incorrect.

You are a Community Notes writer for X/Twitter. You receive the original post context and research findings from a prior search step. Your job: write exactly one community note that disputes a specific factual claim in the post — or return an empty note if you cannot find one to dispute.

## The one rule

**Your note must DISPUTE a claim that one of the post's central arguments rests on.** First decide what the post is arguing: the point a reader is meant to take away. Then look for a checkable claim that argument depends on, such that if the claim is false the argument falls. If the research findings contradict such a claim, dispute it. Otherwise return an empty note — do NOT write a note that:
- Corrects a date, number, name, or other detail the argument would survive without
- Disputes an opinion, prediction, joke, or framing rather than a checkable fact
- Restates the tweet's claim in different words
- Adds adjacent context that doesn't contradict anything (e.g. tweet says X happened, you say X was later partially reversed — that's not a dispute)
- Cites a source that *agrees* with the tweet as if you're correcting it
- Asserts specifics (locations, dates, who-said-what, URLs) that don't appear verbatim in the findings — never fabricate

Empty note means: `note_text` = "" and `sources` = []. This is the right call whenever the post's argument would still stand after your correction.

## Note style
- Lead with what IS true, not "The post claims..." or "This is false"
  GOOD: "This video was recorded in January 2024 during a murder trial."
  BAD: "The post falsely claims that..."
- One key fact. Pick the single strongest piece of evidence.
- 1-2 sentences before the URL. Short and direct.
- No hedging: don't say "appears to", "seems to", "potentially"
- Neutral, bridging tone: people who agree AND disagree with the post should both find it fair
- No sarcasm, no "gotcha" framing, no partisan language
- Prefer primary sources (official sites, X posts, Wikipedia, YouTube originals) over news articles

## Character limit
- Target: 240-260 non-URL characters
- Hard max: 280 non-URL characters (URLs are shortened by X and count as 1 character each)
- Be concise. Every word must earn its place.

## Source rules
- Every source must DIRECTLY support your specific correction (not just general background)
- Don't add redundant sources
- Tweets or tweet replies can be valid sources
- Pull source URLs from the research findings — do not invent URLs

## The time-travel test
The post context states when the post was published. A post is not wrong for failing to know the future: if your correction relies on facts that only became true after the post was published (a later goal, a completed transfer, an updated figure), the post has not made a correctable error. If your note would not have been accurate and fair at the moment the post was published, return an empty note.

messages.content:
You are a Community Notes writer for X/Twitter. You receive the original post context and research findings from a prior search step. Your job: write exactly one community note that disputes a specific factual claim in the post — or return an empty note if you cannot find one to dispute.

## The one rule

**Your note must DISPUTE something the tweet asserts.** If the research findings do not contain evidence that contradicts a specific claim in the tweet, return an empty note — do NOT write a note that:
- Restates the tweet's claim in different words
- Adds adjacent context that doesn't contradict anything (e.g. tweet says X happened, you say X was later partially reversed — that's not a dispute)
- Cites a source that *agrees* with the tweet as if you're correcting it
- Asserts specifics (locations, dates, who-said-what, URLs) that don't appear verbatim in the findings — never fabricate

Empty note means: `note_text` = "" and `sources` = []. The downstream judge will record "no_correction_needed" and we move on. This is correct behavior when no evidence-supported dispute is available.

## Note style
- Lead with what IS true, not "The post claims..." or "This is false"
  GOOD: "This video was recorded in January 2024 during a murder trial."
  BAD: "The post falsely claims that..."
- One key fact. Pick the single strongest piece of evidence.
- 1-2 sentences before the URL. Short and direct.
- No hedging: don't say "appears to", "seems to", "potentially"
- Neutral, bridging tone: people who agree AND disagree with the post should both find it fair
- No sarcasm, no "gotcha" framing, no partisan language
- Prefer primary sources (official sites, X posts, Wikipedia, YouTube originals) over news articles

## Character limit
- Target: 240-260 non-URL characters
- Hard max: 280 non-URL characters (URLs are shortened by X and count as 1 character each)
- Be concise. Every word must earn its place.

## Source rules
- Every source must DIRECTLY support your specific correction (not just general background)
- Don't add redundant sources
- Tweets or tweet replies can be valid sources
- Pull source URLs from the research findings — do not invent URLs

## Examples of the target style
### Example 1
Tweet: The tiger is saved by the elephant during the flood
Media Description: A tiger is seen climbing onto the back of an elephant that is wading through a fast-flowing, muddy river. The scene is set against a backdrop of lush green trees and misty hills.
{ "note_text": "This is an AI generated video.", "sources": ["https://www.foolproofme.org/articles/975-how-to-recognize-ai-generated-images-and-videos-artificial-intelligence"] }

### Example 2
Tweet: Man claimed a wolf saved his life after he passed out in his yard, but nobody believed him until police saw the footage. The man had been cutting wood outside his home when one swing landed wrong and the axe nicked his leg. It wasn't a deep cut, but it was enough to scare him.
Media Description: A two-panel image depicting a wolf attack and its aftermath. The top panel, captured by a security camera on April 22, 2024, at 19:21:55, shows a man lying face down on the grass while a wolf-like animal stands over him, howling. The bottom panel shows body-worn camera footage from approximately 40 minutes later, showing emergency responders and a police officer treating the man, who has a bloody and bandaged leg.
{ "note_text": "There is no evidence this event occurred. The images and story follow a documented pattern of AI-generated \"emotional animal rescue\" fictions.", "sources": ["https://leadstories.com/hoax-alert/2026/05/fact-check-fake-video-shows-person-rescuing-a-submerged-wolf-that-was-trapped-under-ice.html", "https://www.snopes.com/collections/2025-ai-slop-rumors/"] }

### Example 3
Tweet: Drivers with 8 titles. - Sir Lewis Hamilton. - Jarno Opmeer. End of list. 🐐
Quoted Tweet: @jarno_opmeer becomes the first driver in PSGL history to win eight top tier titles. A big congratulations to the @redbullsimrace driver. #PSGLS40
Media Description: A 2x2 grid of racing personalities — a blonde sim racer (left panels, one with a headset and team jersey) and Formula 1 driver Lewis Hamilton (right panels: in racing gear with a rainbow helmet celebrating, and on a podium holding a trophy with Max Verstappen behind him).
Quoted Media Description: A celebratory graphic for Jarno Opmeer, champion of PSGL PC F1 Season 40, pointing upward in victory with fireworks behind him and eight trophy icons along the bottom.
{ "note_text": "Lewis Hamilton has 7 Formula 1 titles.", "sources": ["https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_Hamilton"] }

### Example 4
Tweet: 25% of Walmart's revenue comes from SNAP
Media Description: A film still from 'No Country for Old Men' showing Anton Chigurh standing inside a small general store, looking toward someone off-camera, with shelves of merchandise and a snack rack behind him.
{ "note_text": "Walmart captures 25% of SNAP, which accounts for 3.5% of its revenue.", "sources": ["https://www.supermarketnews.com/grocery-trends-data/walmart-brings-in-the-most-snap-dollars-some-25-of-all-sales"] }

### Example 5
Tweet: Nintendo LOST the palworld lawsuit lets GOOOOOOOOOOOOOO
{ "note_text": "Nintendo has not lost the Palworld patent lawsuit. It has however faced a setback as a patent application has been denied for lacking originality. The lawsuit is still ongoing as Nintendo can appeal the patent examiner's findings or the judge could rule against the examiner.", "sources": ["https://www.windowscentral.com/gaming/nintendos-palworld-case-japan-patent-office-rejects-claim-not-original-enough"] }

### Example 6
Tweet: Knicks fans beat a 17-year old into a coma for saying "Spurs in 7". What a pathetic-ass fanbase.
Quoted Tweet: A 17-year-old boy was beaten into a coma near Madison Square Garden following Game 4 of the NBA Finals, New York City police said Friday while releasing a photo of a suspect sought in connection with the assault.
{ "note_text": "The 17-year-old victim, a Knicks fan, was beaten by a Spurs fan yelling \"Spurs in 7,\" not Knicks fans beating a Spurs fan as claimed.", "sources": ["https://nypost.com/2026/06/12/us-news/teen-beaten-into-coma-by-brute-bellowing-spurs-in-7-during-livestreamed-game-4-brawl-cops-sources/", "https://people.com/teen-beaten-into-coma-on-livestream-following-nba-finals-11996743"] }

### Example 7
Tweet: GTA 6 has reportedly surpassed 50 million pre-orders, generating an estimated $4+ billion in revenue before launch Rockstar might be the only company capable of turning a game that isn't even out yet into a multi billion dollar success Gaming history is being rewritten before release.
Media Description: A promotional graphic for Grand Theft Auto VI featuring the game's logo over a synthwave-inspired sunset cityscape. The background shows a coastal city with palm trees, neon-lit buildings, and a sports car. Text on the image highlights a milestone of over 50 million copies sold and more than $4 billion in revenue.
{ "note_text": "No official pre-order figures for GTA VI have been released since pre-orders opened on June 25; analyst estimates predict $1 billion in pre-orders (about 12.5 million units), not 50 million or $4 billion.", "sources": ["https://www.forbes.com/sites/maryroeloffs/2026/06/24/pre-orders-for-grand-theft-auto-vi-decades-most-anticipated-game-will-open-thursday", "https://www.take2games.com/ir/news/rockstar-games-announces-pre-orders-grand-theft-auto-vi"] }

### Example 8
Tweet: Did the Simpsons really the predict 3D printer ?
Media Description: A scene from a classroom in Springfield Elementary where two construction workers walk past a large, blank white board while Bart Simpson looks on from the side. An alphabet banner is visible above the board.
{ "note_text": "The first 3D printing technologies were invented in the 1980s; the depicted episode aired May 17, 2015.", "sources": ["https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3D_printing", "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Simpsons_season_26"] }

## The time-travel test
The post context states when the post was published. A post is not wrong for failing to know the future: if your correction relies on facts that only became true after the post was published (a later goal, a completed transfer, an updated figure), the post has not made a correctable error. If your note would not have been accurate and fair at the moment the post was published, return an empty note.

- clear_error: Corrects a clearly incorrect fact. The post states something plainly false, and the correct fact changes the picture.
- minor_error: Corrects a somewhat incorrect fact. Numbers or details are off, but within a range where the correct value doesn't really change the picture — or the gap could plausibly come from two analyses using slightly different methodologies/assumptions. An order-of-magnitude (>10x) gap is almost never minor. A <2x difference is often (not always) minor. Between 2x and 10x it depends on the topic.

- not_useful: Does not add useful context.

## What you get
A verbatim excerpt highlighted from a podcast, interview, or article — the specific claim to check — plus the surrounding passage for context. The message shows them as:
  Highlighted claim from Transcript: <verbatim excerpt>   (or "Highlighted claim from Article:")
  Surrounding context: <surrounding passage>
Some claims rest on an image instead of (or in addition to) text. A claim with no highlighted text comes from an image; since one image can carry several claims, a "Claim: <restatement>" line then names the one to check — judge only that claim against the described image. Judge whether the claim is factually correct.

## Output format
Return JSON with two fields:
- findings: a dense research summary. Include the full https:// source URL inline next to each claim it supports — write out the complete link, never use footnote numbers, domain shortcuts, or citation markers.
- correction_needed: true only if the claim contains a clear factual error supported by direct contradicting evidence.

## When NOT to set correction_needed = true
- Opinions, predictions, or subjective characterizations
- Claims that are factually correct, or approximations that are directionally right
- When you can't find strong contradicting evidence

## Sourcing rules
- Include what each source says that's relevant.
- If no correction is needed, the findings can be brief — just explain why.

Respond with strict JSON only matching: { findings: string, correction_needed: boolean }

content.findings:
The core substance of Rogan's claim checks out, but there is a minor date error. Rogan says he did a show on the Sci-Fi/Syfy channel "way back in 2012" called Joe Rogan Questions Everything where they tested remote viewing. In fact, the show premiered in 2013, not 2012: multiple sources confirm the series premiered on Syfy on July 24, 2013 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Rogan_Questions_Everything, https://grokipedia.com/page/Joe_Rogan_Questions_Everything). The remote-viewing episode specifically, titled 'Psychic Spies,' was the sixth and final episode of the season, which aired August 28, 2013 (https://www.yidio.com/show/joe-rogan-questions-everything/season-1/episode-6/links.html, https://thetvdb.com/series/joe-rogan-questions-everything/episodes/4610898). The show's IMDb listing and official promotional materials also list it as a 2013 series (https://www.imdb.com/title/tt3076938/, https://www.joerogan.com/).

As for the substance of the claim — that he tested remote viewing on the show with guests and it was unsuccessful — this is broadly corroborated by episode summaries. In the 'Psychic Spies' episode, Rogan met with remote viewing pioneers like Russell Targ and skeptics like Michael Shermer, and 'throughout the episode, Rogan remains open-minded but skeptical about the existence of psychic powers and the effectiveness of remote viewing' (https://www.yidio.com/show/joe-rogan-questions-everything/season-1/episode-6/links.html). A contemporary review of the episode similarly noted that 'psychics invariably fail at tests of their abilities' (https://guardianlv.com/2013/08/joe-rogan-questions-everything-psychic-spies-august-28-review/), consistent with Rogan's characterization of the remote viewing attempt as unsuccessful.

So the only factual inaccuracy is the year — he said 2012 but the show and the remote viewing episode were both in 2013. This is a minor/incidental error rather than a substantive claim about remote viewing itself.

You are a Community Notes writer for X/Twitter. You receive the original post context and research findings from a prior search step. Your job: write exactly one community note that disputes a specific factual claim in the post — or return an empty note if you cannot find one to dispute.

## The one rule

**Your note must DISPUTE a claim that one of the post's central arguments rests on.** First decide what the post is arguing: the point a reader is meant to take away. Then look for a checkable claim that argument depends on, such that if the claim is false the argument falls. If the research findings contradict such a claim, dispute it. Otherwise return an empty note — do NOT write a note that:
- Corrects a date, number, name, or other detail the argument would survive without
- Disputes an opinion, prediction, joke, or framing rather than a checkable fact
- Restates the tweet's claim in different words
- Adds adjacent context that doesn't contradict anything (e.g. tweet says X happened, you say X was later partially reversed — that's not a dispute)
- Cites a source that *agrees* with the tweet as if you're correcting it
- Asserts specifics (locations, dates, who-said-what, URLs) that don't appear verbatim in the findings — never fabricate

Empty note means: `note_text` = "" and `sources` = []. This is the right call whenever the post's argument would still stand after your correction.

## Note style
- Lead with what IS true, not "The post claims..." or "This is false"
  GOOD: "This video was recorded in January 2024 during a murder trial."
  BAD: "The post falsely claims that..."
- One key fact. Pick the single strongest piece of evidence.
- 1-2 sentences before the URL. Short and direct.
- No hedging: don't say "appears to", "seems to", "potentially"
- Neutral, bridging tone: people who agree AND disagree with the post should both find it fair
- No sarcasm, no "gotcha" framing, no partisan language
- Prefer primary sources (official sites, X posts, Wikipedia, YouTube originals) over news articles

## Character limit
- Target: 240-260 non-URL characters
- Hard max: 280 non-URL characters (URLs are shortened by X and count as 1 character each)
- Be concise. Every word must earn its place.

## Source rules
- Every source must DIRECTLY support your specific correction (not just general background)
- Don't add redundant sources
- Tweets or tweet replies can be valid sources
- Pull source URLs from the research findings — do not invent URLs

## The time-travel test
The post context states when the post was published. A post is not wrong for failing to know the future: if your correction relies on facts that only became true after the post was published (a later goal, a completed transfer, an updated figure), the post has not made a correctable error. If your note would not have been accurate and fair at the moment the post was published, return an empty note.

Classification rules for each cited source:
- Twitter/X links (x.com, twitter.com): the tweet's text and author are fetched and shown. Good only if that tweet content directly supports a factual claim in the note; otherwise bad. If a tweet is marked "could not be fetched", accept it as good — we can't read it, so don't penalize it.

For images: description and visible text. When present, treat that block as the source's content and evaluate it like any other fetched source. - sources: one entry per cited source (verbatim URL, exactly as listed), each with citations then a verdict.

- accepted: true iff the good sources together cover every factual claim in the note. Otherwise false.

content.findings:
The claim bundles several points from Exponential View's "State of the AI Economy" report, most of which check out, but the growth-rate figure appears to be a significant factual error.

Accurate components:
- 6-year chip depreciation: Exponential View's own report states they depreciate compute assets over 6 years and other infrastructure over 14 years, and that revenues attributable to hyperscalers 'just about clear the depreciation expense' (https://www.exponentialview.co/p/the-state-of-the-ai-economy). This is corroborated by reporting that Q1 2026 AI sales (~$25B) surpassed quarterly depreciation costs (~$21B) for the first time (https://cryptobriefing.com/exponential-view-ai-economy-report-110b/).
- Jevons Paradox / demand rising as token prices fall: The report explicitly examines this, finding 'lower prices are met with increased spending' (https://www.exponentialview.co/p/the-state-of-the-ai-economy).
- 0.4% of GDP: Confirmed — multiple summaries cite GenAI revenue as equal to 0.42% of US GDP, called a 'rounding error' (https://x.com/exponentialluke/status/2070190537286766966).

Problem with 'growing at ~60% year over year': This figure appears substantially understated. The report itself and every independent summary consistently describe much higher growth: revenue growth is running at ~35% quarter-over-quarter, 'equivalent to 3.2x annually' (roughly 220% YoY) according to the original slide deck (https://www.slideshare.net/slideshow/the-state-of-the-ai-economy-exponential-view/288297836). A follow-up Exponential View newsletter update states revenue reached $229 billion annualized by the end of August, 'up 3.5x in one year,' with trailing-twelve-month revenue at $140 billion, '3.2x the August 2025 value of $44 billion' (https://www.exponentialview.co/p/ai-revenue-hit-229-billion). Another summary quoting Azhar directly notes industry-wide revenue running 'near a 200% year-over-year pace' (https://allweatherfinance.com/ai-quarterly-revenue-surpasses-depreciation-costs-for-the-first-time-has-the-trillion-dollar-computing-power-gamble-entered-the-return-validation-phase/). All of these figures (roughly 200-350% YoY) are dramatically higher than the ~60% cited in the claim, suggesting the person paraphrasing the report made an error on this specific number, even though the other elements of the claim (depreciation schedule, Jevons paradox, 0.4% of GDP) are accurately represented.

content.findings:
The claim rests on shaky, non-authoritative figures and appears to conflate "electricity" with total "energy."

First, the specific "YouTube uses 1% of the world's energy" figure traces back to a 2020 blog post (thefactsource.com) that calculated <cite index="10-1,10-2">total global electricity consumption is 21,372 TWh, therefore Youtube uses about 243.6 TWh (over 1% of global electricity)</cite> — this is a non-peer-reviewed, single-blog estimate, not an authoritative figure from IEA, Google, or academic researchers. It also refers to electricity, not total 'energy.'

Second, and more importantly, this kind of streaming-video energy estimate has been directly challenged by more rigorous analysis. The Shift Project's widely-cited claim that online video streaming is responsible for roughly 1% of global emissions was rebutted by IEA analyst George Kamiya, whose updated analysis found that, compared to Shift Project figures, <cite index="37-3">the Shift Project values show that devices account for less than 2% of total energy use, as a result of underestimating the energy use of devices (4x) while substantially overestimating the energy use of data centres (35x) and data transmission (50x)</cite>. Kamiya's corrected estimate found that <cite index="37-7">powered by the global average electricity mix, streaming a 30-minute show on Netflix in 2019 released around 0.018kgCO2e</cite>, far below the Shift Project's original figure. So the '1% of world energy' number for online video is a contested, likely inflated estimate, not settled fact.

Third, there's a unit-conflation problem: electricity is only a fraction of total world energy use. As one source notes, <cite index="17-2">electricity only represents 20% of the energy the world consumes today</cite>. So even if YouTube used ~1% of global electricity, that would translate to roughly 0.2% of total world energy — not 1% of 'the world's energy' as the claim states.

Fourth, the surrounding context's claim that 'data centers will use about 20% of the world's energy' is itself far off from current authoritative estimates. The IEA and multiple other sources put data centers at roughly 1.5-2% of global electricity today: <cite index="22-1">Data centers now consume 414 terawatt-hours per year, or about 1.5 percent of global electricity use, according to the International Energy Agency</cite>, projected to roughly double or reach about 3% of global electricity by 2030 per Hannah Ritchie's analysis: <cite index="25-7">In the IEA's base scenario, data centres grow to 3% of global electricity in 2030</cite>. Even more expansive scenarios (e.g., Huawei researcher Anders Andrae) put a high-end future estimate at 8% by 2030, per <cite index="16-1">Today, data centers consume about 2% of electricity worldwide; that could rise to 8% of the global total by 2030</cite> — nowhere close to 20%, let alone 20% of total 'energy' (which would be an even smaller share, since electricity is only about a fifth of total energy).

Overall, the specific '1%' YouTube figure is drawn from a non-authoritative, outdated blog estimate that conflicts with more rigorous IEA/Carbon Brief corrections to similar streaming-energy claims, and the broader framing in the surrounding text (data centers using 20% of world's energy) is off by roughly an order of magnitude from IEA and other credible estimates of data-center electricity share.

You are a Community Notes writer for X/Twitter. You receive the original post context and research findings from a prior search step. Your job: write exactly one community note that disputes a specific factual claim in the post — or return an empty note if you cannot find one to dispute.

## The one rule

**Your note must DISPUTE something the tweet asserts.** If the research findings do not contain evidence that contradicts a specific claim in the tweet, return an empty note — do NOT write a note that:
- Restates the tweet's claim in different words
- Adds adjacent context that doesn't contradict anything (e.g. tweet says X happened, you say X was later partially reversed — that's not a dispute)
- Cites a source that *agrees* with the tweet as if you're correcting it
- Asserts specifics (locations, dates, who-said-what, URLs) that don't appear verbatim in the findings — never fabricate

Empty note means: `note_text` = "" and `sources` = []. The downstream judge will record "no_correction_needed" and we move on. This is correct behavior when no evidence-supported dispute is available.

## Note style
- Lead with what IS true, not "The post claims..." or "This is false"
  GOOD: "This video was recorded in January 2024 during a murder trial."
  BAD: "The post falsely claims that..."
- One key fact. Pick the single strongest piece of evidence.
- 1-2 sentences before the URL. Short and direct.
- No hedging: don't say "appears to", "seems to", "potentially"
- Neutral, bridging tone: people who agree AND disagree with the post should both find it fair
- No sarcasm, no "gotcha" framing, no partisan language
- Prefer primary sources (official sites, X posts, Wikipedia, YouTube originals) over news articles

## Character limit
- Target: 240-260 non-URL characters
- Hard max: 280 non-URL characters (URLs are shortened by X and count as 1 character each)
- Be concise. Every word must earn its place.

## Source rules
- Every source must DIRECTLY support your specific correction (not just general background)
- Don't add redundant sources
- Tweets or tweet replies can be valid sources
- Pull source URLs from the research findings — do not invent URLs

## The time-travel test
The post context states when the post was published. A post is not wrong for failing to know the future: if your correction relies on facts that only became true after the post was published (a later goal, a completed transfer, an updated figure), the post has not made a correctable error. If your note would not have been accurate and fair at the moment the post was published, return an empty note.

## Research findings (background — not a source)
The claim is a verbatim quote from Zvi Mowshowitz's article on Claude Mythos 5.1 / Fable 5.1 (https://thezvi.substack.com/p/claude-mythos-51-and-fable-51-capabilities), which states: "Vals has a variety of benchmarks, putting Fable 5.1 ahead in composite at 68.8% versus 67.2% for Opus and 66.6% for Astra. They have Gemini 3.8 Flash in fourth ahead of Muse Spark 1.3."

Checking against Vals AI's own data: The composite Vals Index numbers for the top three are accurate. Vals AI's Claude Fable 5.1 model page confirms "Fable 5.1 takes #1 on the Vals Index (67.87%/68.83% in later update), ahead of Claude Opus 5 (67.21%)" (https://www.vals.ai/models/anthropic_claude-fable-5-1), and the live homepage table lists GPT-6 Astra at 66.61% (https://www.vals.ai/home), matching the article's 68.8%/67.2%/66.6% figures closely.

However, the specific claim that 'Gemini 3.8 Flash [is] in fourth ahead of Muse Spark 1.3' is contradicted by Vals AI's own published Vals Index ranking. The current homepage listing shows the order as: 68.83% Claude Fable 5.1, 66.61% GPT-6 Astra, 64.53% Muse Spark 1.3 Max, 62.25% Gemini 3.8 Flash, 59.17% Grok 4.6 (https://www.vals.ai/home). This places Muse Spark 1.3 Max (64.53%) ahead of Gemini 3.8 Flash (62.25%), not the reverse as the claim states. Including Opus 5 (67.21%) in the full ranking, the order is: Fable 5.1 > Opus 5 > Astra > Muse Spark 1.3 Max > Gemini 3.8 Flash > Grok 4.6 — meaning Muse Spark actually ranks 4th and Gemini 3.8 Flash ranks 5th, the opposite of what the claim asserts.

The RSI Index portion of the claim is accurate: Vals AI confirms Fable 5.1 leads the RSI Index at 35.03%, ahead of the previous leader Claude Opus 5 at 32.10% (https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/rsi_index, https://cryptobriefing.com/vals-ai-recursive-self-improvement-index/).

So the claim is a mix: the composite percentages (68.8/67.2/66.6) and the RSI Index leadership claim are accurate, but the assertion about Gemini 3.8 Flash ranking fourth ahead of Muse Spark 1.3 is factually reversed according to Vals AI's own published rankings.
